newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN chief urges compromise in Abkhazia dispute.
newsitem.headline: UN chief urges compromise in Abkhazia dispute.

text.p: United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan urged Georgia and its rebel province Abkhazia on Wednesday to work for compromises to put an end to a sovereignty dispute that has cost at least 10,000 lives.

Annan's message was read to delegations from both sides by his special representative Liviu Bota at the formal opening of three days of U.N.-sponsored talks aimed at finding a way out of a four-year stalemate.
"The primary responsibility for resolving the differences and finding a lasting political settlement rests with the two sides," Annan said.

Assistance in the form of ideas, technical and humanitarian help, economic support and on maintaining peacekeeping forces and U.N. observers in the region could come from others in the international community.
"But it is up to the two parties themselves to develop direct dialogue and to make the necessary compromises to achieve a lasting settlement," the U.N. chief declared.

The dispute, which simmered for years under the old Soviet Union when Georgia was a Soviet republic and Abkhazia was an autonomous republic within Georgia, is one of several left over after the breakup in 1991 of the old communist superpower.

The talks, the first under the umbrella of the world body for over two years, come just a week before the mandate runs out for a force of 1,500 Russian peacekeepers in a buffer zone along the de facto frontier between Georgia and Abkhazia.

Georgian President and former Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze has just been in Washington and at the United Nations in New York seeking support for the deployment of a multinational force to replace the Russians.
He says if that is not forthcoming then the Russians must agree to police a wider zone and help Georgians driven from Abkhazia during the 1992-93 conflict in the region to return.
If Moscow declines, Shevardnadze has warned, the Russian force must leave. But so far Russia has refused, saying the Abkhaz must also agree to a new mandate for the force.

Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba told Reuters in his capital Sukhumi this week that his administration -- which initially sought full independence -- would not accept an international force and warned his forces would repel any Georgian attack.

The Geneva talks, due to continue until Friday, are being held at a relatively low level with Georgia, recognised by the international community, sending its Foreign Minister Irakly Mengarishvili and Abkhazia, which has won no formal recognition abroad, its top foreign affairs official Sergei Shamba.

Also attending is a delegation from Russia, which has promoted earlier efforts to achieving a settlement, officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), and from the United States, Britain, France and Germany.
